We must therefore say that if the dialectical conception of the human being could not account for human beings as “persons,” it would not be fully true. All the more so if it were actually incompatible with the existence of personality.
But that is not the case.
If we recognize the dialectical character of human existence, we must also recognize human “individuality.”
In other words, a human being is an individual precisely because they are dialectical—that is, synthetic—and therefore necessarily contain the moments of both thesis and antithesis.
We can show this as follows.
Let us first assume, without proof, that every individual being is both finite and free, and that conversely every finite and free being is individual.
If we grant this, then individuality and dialectical existence turn out to be one and the same thing.

Freedom is nothing other than “negativity,” or the antithetical aspect. Finitude, or mortality, belongs to every living natural being and therefore to the animal that underlies human existence—in other words, to the human “body,” in the broad sense.
But the “body,” as we already know, is the original thesis of the human being. Everything th
etical in human existence is ultimately rooted in the body and inseparably attached to it.
We can therefore say that human finitude or mortality belongs to the human being’s th†etical side, just as freedom belongs to the antithetical side.
And since the simultaneous presence of thesis and antithesis necessarily brings synthesis with it, we can say that every synthetic, and therefore dialectical, being is individual.
Conversely, every individual being is dialectical because it necessarily contains both finitude—that is, thesis—and freedom—that is, antithesis—and therefore forms a synthesis.
In other words, dialectic is realized only in the human being.

So we can say, on the one hand, that only a human being is an individual and, on the other hand, that a human being is always an individual—or, equivalently, that a “person” is always and everywhere a “human person.”
But we still have to show that an individual being really must be both finite and free, and that a finite and free being must really be an individual.
First of all, we must emphasize that when we call an “individual” “unique in its kind,” this has to be taken literally.
We mean unique in its kind: unique in its “nature” or “essence,” in its “essential” qualities—not merely in accidental, external, or secondary details.

For, as Leibniz liked to point out, there are no two completely identical things in nature. We cannot find, for example, two oak leaves that are perfectly identical. Yet no one speaks of the “individuality” or “personality” of these leaves.
If human beings differ—or can differ—from one another in an “essential” way, in their essential qualities, then it follows that there is no universal human “essence” or nature.

But human beings remain human despite differing essentially from one another. This means that one can possess any number of different essences and still remain human—or, if you prefer, that what is human is precisely what has no fixed “essence,” what is not bound in its future by what it is and what it has been.
This means that a human being can negate their “essence”—and therefore, strictly speaking, has no such essence.
So to be a “person” or an “individual” one must contain “negativity” and possess the ability to realize it.
And we already know that negativity is nothing other than freedom, while its realization is free action.
The person is therefore always free.
And once we see this, we can also show that the person is finite.
If the human being has no essence, then human “possibilities” are not limited in advance.
A dog can live only “as a dog,” and a cat only “as a cat.” But a human being can live “as a slave,” “as a master,” “as a bourgeois,” “as a proletarian,” “as a revolutionary,” and so on.
In principle, therefore, a human being can live “however they choose.”
The longer a person lives, the more they will normally change.

If they lived infinitely long—that is, if they were immortal—they would eventually realize all of their possibilities. For, as Aristotle rightly observed, a possibility that is never realized, that remains eternally unrealized, is not really a possibility at all but an impossibility.
And all the possibilities of a particular human being are ultimately all human possibilities in general.

For if different people possessed fundamentally different sets of possibilities, those possibilities would have to be limited or determined by something eternal and unchanging. In other words, each person would possess a fixed “nature” or “essence,” which, as we already know, is incompatible with freedom.

So if human beings lived eternally, every one of them would eventually realize all human possibilities. Each would therefore cease not only to differ essentially from the others but would become completely identical with them.
We can therefore say that if a person must necessarily be free, they must also be finite—that is, mortal.
Conversely, an infinite or eternal, immortal being cannot be free, and therefore cannot be a person either.

This is obvious if we imagine eternal beings that differ essentially from one another. For that would mean that the possibilities of each were “determined” or “bounded.” Each would possess an eternal and unchanging “nature” or “essence,” and freedom is incompatible with such an essence.
But the same remains true even if we suppose that all eternal beings are identical.
Insofar as a being is eternal, it has already realized “from all eternity” all of its possibilities.

Even if those possibilities were infinite—assuming that such an actual realization of infinity were possible—the totality of its infinite realized possibilities would still constitute an eternal and unchanging, though infinite, “essence” or nature. The being could neither change nor, still less, negate that nature.
So there would once again be no room for negativity, and therefore no room for freedom, in such an infinite or eternal being.
We must therefore say that a person is always finite.
But the converse is clearly not true.
We cannot say that every finite being is an individual or “person.” Animals are unquestionably finite and mortal, yet we do not regard them as persons.
So an individual being must possess something in addition to finitude: namely, as we already know, freedom.
We can say that an animal dies—comes to an “end”—once it has exhausted or realized all of its possibilities. Or, if you prefer, it perishes because it has realized them.

Take a female cat. From the embryo onward, she develops continuously until she reaches full sexual maturity. Once she has conceived another embryo and given birth to a kitten, she has, in a sense, “nothing more to say to the world.”
After that she can only repeat what she has already done. She herself no longer changes in any essential way.
Her continued existence therefore has, so to speak, no further “meaning” or “justification,” either for others or for herself. It is as though her death simply belongs “to the order of things.”
And the fact that she really has exhausted all of her “cat possibilities” is revealed and confirmed by the fact that she does not differ essentially from her offspring.

The natural cycle that begins with an embryo and ends with a new embryo remains eternally unchanged, at least as long as we are dealing with this particular animal species, and it repeats itself indefinitely.
As Aristotle rightly observed, this cycle is itself nothing other than the realization in time and space of an animal’s “essence” or “nature”—what Plato called its “Idea.”

We can therefore say that animals are not “individuals”: their offspring simply reproduce or repeat their parents. And this is ultimately because animals possess an eternal and unchanging “nature” and are therefore not free.

Insofar as a person is free—insofar as they possess unlimited or “infinite” possibilities—they always die, so to speak, too soon: prematurely, in the middle of the journey, in what we might call an unnatural or “violent” death. Nature kills them.
However long a person’s finite life may last, they can never realize within it all of their infinite possibilities.

They therefore always have, in a sense, the “right” to more life. In principle, if they continued living, they could still bring something new into the world. Additional life would therefore still have a “meaning” and a “justification,” both for the person and for the world around them.
This is why a human being can be an incomparable “person”: an individual who is “one of a kind.”
If human beings can “choose” among unlimited possibilities, each person can choose a possibility that no one else has ever chosen.
They can therefore always differ from every other person.
And this is what it means to be an incomparable person.

For an individual is not someone who tries at all costs to resemble no one else simply for the pleasure of being different. An individual is someone who possesses the possibility of being one of a kind, even if in many respects they are in fact like everyone else.
We can therefore say, in general, that “personal” or “individual” existence is existence that is finite in its actuality but unlimited in its possibilities.
And that, as we already know, means an existence that is simultaneously mortal and free.
We can add one more point.

The unlimited character of human possibilities—or, more exactly, the fact that a person dies before having had time to exhaust all their possibilities—is revealed or “proved” by the fact that human existence is not cyclical.

The human body, like the body of any animal, reproduces itself only through descendants. But properly human life does not stand still. In principle, the son does not merely repeat the father; he goes “further” than the father.
And we can say that a person’s “spiritual descendants,” who obviously need not be their biological children, realize possibilities that the person themselves “did not manage” to realize.
But we have already explained that human existence is not “cyclical,” as animal existence is. It is historical.
So any being that is finite “in actuality” but infinite “in potentiality” is nothing other than a “worldly, free, and historical” being.
In a word, it is a human being—and therefore also an “individual” or “person.”
We can therefore say not only that every “person” is necessarily free and finite, and therefore historical, but also that every finite and free—that is, historical—being is necessarily a “person.”
So to say that a human being is an “individual” and to say that a human being is “synthetic,” or dialectical, is to say the same thing in different words.

That is why, once we have said that the human being is dialectical—that is, that human existence simultaneously contains all three dialectical aspects, thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—we can also say that the human being is a “free and historical person.”
To summarize, let us repeat the point once more.

In every form of human existence—whether in an individual person, in the human community as a whole, or even in any product of human activity—we can distinguish three aspects at work in the dialectic.
There is the thesis, in which “identity” predominates.
There is the antithesis, in which negativity predominates.
And there is the synthesis, in which “totality” predominates.
In reality, however, these aspects are inseparable.
The real human being is always a synthesis in the broad sense of the term. Human existence necessarily contains, alongside synthesis in the narrower sense, thesis and antithesis as well.

But as we have already seen, this real, general “synthesis” can itself function as a “thesis” in relation to another “synthesis” that plays the role of antithesis and, together with the thesis, produces a further synthetic synthesis.
In other words, every synthesis—every human existence or human entity, and everything made by human beings—can serve as the starting point of a dialectical process.
It can become a “thesis” that is abolished by an “antithesis” but preserved within a new “synthesis,” and so on.
When we speak about dialectic and dialectical existence, therefore, we have to approach the question from two different angles.
On the one hand, we can consider one and the same entity, or one and the same stage in its development over time.
From this perspective, the entity or stage is dialectical when it contains all three aspects—thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—simultaneously and in practice inseparably.

On the other hand, there can also be a dialectical relation between different entities, or between different stages in the development of one and the same entity. This relation allows us to arrange them in the order thesis, antithesis, synthesis.
In this case, the three can exist separately. They follow one another in time—in the kind of time ruled by the future, that is, by antithesis or “negativity.”
We will therefore call these entities dialectical as well, while calling the relation between them the real dialectic in the proper sense of the term.
We now know, at least to some extent, what the real dialectic described by the philosophical system of Hegelian Marxism—and in particular by Hegelian-Marxist Phenomenology—actually is.
We know that it is not a method but a reality.
And we also know that the philosophical method is nothing other than the method of giving a pure description of actuality.

If this description is “dialectical,” that is only because it reflects the dialectical structure of actuality with photographic precision, like a mirror. That structure exists in reality independently of its philosophical description.
If this is so—if the philosophical description of the real dialectic reflects its actual structure—then the description itself must also be divided along the two lines we have just distinguished.
Philosophy will describe, on the one hand, the dialectical aspects of actuality and, on the other hand, its dialectical stages: the dialectic in the proper sense, the real dialectic itself.
In actuality, as we know, the different aspects exist inseparably and simultaneously.
So if philosophy describes them separately, and even one after another, this is only because we cannot speak about everything at once or say everything in a single instant.
In this respect, the philosophical description of dialectical actuality does not, if you like, coincide perfectly with actuality itself.
